newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Telecom shares surge on buyback rumours.
newsitem.headline: Telecom shares surge on buyback rumours.

text.p: Telecom Corp of New Zealand shares surged 24 cents, or 3.2 percent, to a new all-time high of $7.70 on Thursday as new rumours of a capital reduction resurfaced.
Few brokers or analysts were actually promoting the rumour of the share repurchase but most acknowledged the rumour was doing the rounds.
"The rumours that seem to be flying around are the buyback ones," said ANZ Securities analyst Hugh Ammundsen.
Telecom declined comment on the rumour but a spokesman noted the share price had often run up ahead of its result in the past.
Telecom is due to report first half earnings next Thursday.
Brokers said the share price was very strong in the U.S. overnight as the Dow surged, and it continued to run up in local trade on aggressive buying.

"It would appear there is speculation of a buyback or they are going to do some sort of capital reduction," said Cavill White Securities Head of Research John Cairns. "It's very much the rumour doing the rounds but we have spoken to the company
and it is taken aback by that."

Telecom has a target to keep within a 40-45 percent ratio of net debt to net debt plus equity and was at the bottom end of the range at the end of the first quarter, suggesting it has room to be more aggressively leveraged or to repay capital.
But some analysts said a capital reduction did not tally with the company's heavy capital expenditure programme and payout of a high proportion of total profits.
Ammundsen said Telecom was hovering at the lower end of the target range and a capital reduction decision revolved around the size of Telecom's cap ex programme and tax considerations.

He said the tax consequences of any capital reduction were crucial. Revenue reserves were cleaned out in the previous one for five share cancellation in March 1994 and the issue for shareholders was whether a further reduction would be treated as a realisation of gains rather than a reduction of capital.
He said Telecom would need to get a favourable ruling from the IRD before proceeding with any reduction.
However, Ammundsen said without a reduction Telecom would drop below its 40 percent target and that could be considered an inefficient use of capital.
